column4: The section’s source word muʾṣadah names a closed fire; this ayah repeats مُّؤْصَدَةٌۭ and says it is shut over them, turning the familiar light into an enclosure.
The next ayah adds that the fire is in extended columns (عَمَدٍۢ مُّمَدَّدَةٍۭ); it extends the preceding claim that it is closed over them.
The section contrasts a beacon seen from afar with punishment; this ayah says the fire reaches the hearts, showing its inward reach.
This ayah identifies the enclosed punishment as “the Fire of Allah, kindled” (نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ), complementing the source section’s account of fire as created light and as judgment.
The section’s traveler sees a distant fire as guidance; here the fire sees its deniers from a distant place and roars at them, reversing who sees whom and what the fire does.
The next ayah confines the deniers in a narrow place, chained together; it adds an explicit cramped enclosure to the fire that sees them from afar in 25:12.
The criminals see the Fire, expect to fall into it, and find no escape; this joins the section’s seen-from-afar fire to its final image of enclosure.
The section ends with people unable to leave the closed Fire; this ayah states that they cannot get out of the Fire (بِخَٰرِجِينَ مِنَ ٱلنَّارِ).
The passage names لَظَىٰ, a blazing fire, a direct parallel to the sealed punishment in the section.
The next ayah says this fire strips the scalp; it adds what the fire does to the people it calls in 70:17.
The source section says the closed fire falls on those who reject God’s signs; this ayah says the fire calls those who turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ).
The section connects the fire with people who hoard; this ayah identifies the called person as one who gathered wealth and kept it stored (جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ).
The warning “with a blazing fire” (نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ) is a direct parallel to the section’s fire closing the surah.
This ayah says who will enter the warned fire—only the most wretched; 92:16 specifies that person’s denial and turning away.
The ayah identifies the one who enters as the person who denied and turned away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), echoing the section’s disbelievers under the sealed fire.
The most God-fearing are kept far from the fire, the opposite fate to the deniers under the section’s closed fire.
The person who gives wealth to purify himself contrasts with the section’s hoarder and connects the fire to the surah’s call to give and show mercy.
The giver has no favor to repay; this clarifies that the giving beside the fire-warning in 92:14–18 is not a reciprocal transaction.
The giver seeks the face of his Most High Lord; this supplies the inward aim behind the charitable action contrasted with hoarding in the section.
This ayah asks what brought people to Saqar; 74:43–47 give their answer, so it frames the following fire scene and its causes.
The people in Saqar say they were not among those who prayed; it supplies one cause of entry into the fire being asked about in 74:42.
They say they did not feed the poor, a direct reversal of the section’s feeding of the needy and mercy before its closing fire.
They also say they joined in vain talk with those who indulged in it; this continues their account of the conduct leading to Saqar.
They say they denied the Day of Judgment, a concrete instance of rejecting the signs before the fire in the section.
Their denial lasted until certainty came; this completes the Saqar group’s answer about how they reached the fire.
The warning addresses those who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God’s way, directly linking the section’s amassed wealth to its fire.
The next ayah says the hoarded metals will be heated in Hell and used to brand their foreheads, sides and backs; it gives a bodily punishment for the hoarding in 9:34.
The section describes a fire set to aid travelers; this ayah says God made fire a reminder and provision for travelers (مَتَٰعًا لِّلْمُقْوِينَ).
This ayah asks about the fire people kindle; it introduces the traveler’s useful fire described in 56:73.
The next ayah asks whether people made the tree of that fire or God; it adds divine creation to the fire whose use 56:73 describes.
The ayah brings together seeing, ānastu (ءَانَسْتُ), a fire, and seeking guidance by it (هُدًۭى), exactly the meeting of roots and scene developed in the section.
This ayah introduces the story of Moses with a divine question; 20:10 supplies the actual distant-fire scene that the question opens.
After Moses comes to the fire, this ayah says he is called; it continues the scene and shows the fire as the setting for divine guidance.
The ayah has Moses say ānastu (ءَانَسْتُ) when he notices a fire and promises a brand or news, with warmth as its use (تَصْطَلُونَ).
This ayah continues the fire scene: when Moses reaches it, he is called and the place is blessed; it adds the transition from finding a fire to receiving a call.
The next ayah identifies the caller as Allah addressing Moses; it completes the divine call begun at the fire in 27:8.
Moses notices a fire at the side of the Mount (آنَسَ ... نَارًا) and hopes to bring news or a burning brand to warm his family, another direct version of the section’s scene.
When Moses reaches the fire, this ayah says he is called from the blessed side of the valley; it continues the fire scene into revelation.
The source dictionary’s root ḥ-s-b links “he supposes” to a fire from the sky; this ayah uses حُسْبَانًا مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ for a calamity that burns up the garden.
The disbelievers are explicitly assigned to Hellfire and abide there; this directly parallels the section’s disbelievers under a sealed fire.
The disbelievers’ fire does not end in death or relief from punishment, extending the section’s closed fire into lasting confinement.
This ayah says Hell will encompass the disbelievers, a specific enclosure parallel to the fire closed over them in the section.
The ayah places a bed from Hell beneath them and coverings above them; this presents the punishment as surrounding them from both sides.
The men on the heights recognize people by their marks across a barrier between Garden and Fire; this connects the section’s high-place signal and the two opposed destinies.
The people on the heights turn their eyes toward the companions of the Fire and ask not to be placed with wrongdoers; it continues the boundary scene of 7:46.
The men on the heights call to people they recognize and ask what their gathering and arrogance availed them; this ties the fire-bound scene to the section’s boast about heaps of wealth.
The call turns to the people presumed unworthy of mercy and tells them to enter the Garden; it completes the split between the two groups in 7:46–48.
God makes the stars signs by which people find their way through the darkness of land and sea, a direct parallel to a high light serving a night traveler.
The ayah names landmarks (عَلَٰمَٰتٍ) and stars as means of guidance, matching the section’s raised fire and road-sign.
This ayah says roads are made so people may be guided; it supplies the path that the landmarks and stars of 16:16 illuminate.
God makes mountain pathways so people may be guided, a physical route parallel to the section’s high route-marker.
The ayah says God makes roads so people may be guided, a direct formulation of the wayfinding function assigned to the fire in the section.
The question asks who guides people in the darknesses of land and sea and sends winds as good news; it joins night guidance with a sign before mercy.
The parable joins light (نُور) to a lamp kindled by a tree, whose oil nearly shines even without fire; it develops the section’s root link between fire and illumination.
The fire first illuminates its surroundings, then its light is taken away and people are left in darkness unable to see, a precise reversal of the fire that guides travelers.
This ayah announces a light (نُور) and a clear Book from God; 5:16 says what that light does as guidance.
The light leads its followers out of darkness into light and guides them to a straight path, matching the section’s beacon-as-guidance image.
The Book brings people from darkness to light and then to a path, an explicit light-and-way parallel to the section’s road beacon.
The revelation is made a light by which God guides people and leads to a straight path, joining the section’s named light and guidance roots.
The people follow the light sent with the Messenger; this parallels the section’s beacon lit so travelers can follow it.
A person given light walks among people by it; this makes light a means of moving through the world, as in the section’s traveler following a fire.
The believers’ light runs before them and on their right as they proceed, a guiding light on the way that contrasts with the section’s fire shut over its occupants.
The next ayah has hypocrites ask for the believers’ light, then a barrier is placed between them; it gives a boundary between those with guiding light and those left outside.
The believers’ light runs before them and on their right, a repeated image of light accompanying people as they move.
When night covers Abraham, he sees a star; this puts a visible light against night’s covering, like the section’s fire seen in darkness.
The day displays the sun; the next ayah gives the reversal of night covering it, matching the section’s contrast between visible fire and concealing night.
The source section glosses night as covering by darkness; this ayah presents the night covering the sun, the direct opposite of a fire visible in darkness.
This surah begins with night as it covers, the darkness against which the warning fire in 92:14 is later heard.
The next oath turns to day as it appears; it completes the night-covering/daylight contrast before the same surah’s fire warning.
The ayah says night wraps over day and day over night (يُكَوِّرُ); it gives a concrete covering image for the section’s night-etymology.
Night is made a garment and sleep a rest, with day as rising again; it joins the section’s covering night and the dictionary sense of fire as a place to rest.
The night is made a rest (سَكَنًا) while sun and moon mark time; this is a related use of the section’s named s-k-n root, though the ayah assigns rest to night rather than fire.
The night is made for people to rest and the day visible; it joins the dictionary’s rest sense with the section’s night scene and fire’s visibility.
The ayah pairs night as a place to rest (لِيَسْكُنُوا۟ فِيهِ) with day made visible, echoing the section’s linked rest, night, and sight.
God makes night and day so people may rest in one and seek bounty in the other; this develops the rest sense of the source’s s-k-n dictionary note.
The night is for rest and day is visible, another direct formulation of the rest-and-sight pairing surrounding the section’s night fire.
Sleep is made a rest (سُبَاتًا), a specific rest-language parallel to the source dictionary’s fire as something one rests by.
The next ayah calls night a covering (لِبَاسًا), matching the source section’s account of night concealing by darkness.
The people on the left face scorching wind and boiling water, a reversal of the useful fire that lets a traveler rest.
The next ayah adds the shade of black smoke to their punishment, continuing the reversal of a fire’s sheltering or resting use.
The smoke is neither cool nor beneficial; this completes the reversal of the source’s dictionary sense of a fire one rests by.
